fields.description: A-level results day, Emma's arrival, and the collapse of Dante's university plans.
fields.content_html:
The Morning Everything Changes

The novel opens on one of the most significant days of Dante Bridgeman's life: the morning of his A-level results. At seventeen, Dante has a clear vision of his future. He wants to study journalism at university — a goal that feels within reach as he waits for the envelope that will confirm his place. His younger brother Adam narrates the opening passages in parallel, and the dual narration is Blackman's central structural device: two brothers, two sets of preoccupations, one household about to be shaken by the same shock.

Dante's results are good. For a brief moment, the future he planned seems confirmed. Then the doorbell rings.

Emma Arrives

At the door is Emma Bryce — Dante's ex-girlfriend, with whom he split up approximately a year earlier. She is not alone. She has arrived with a baby girl in a pushchair. The baby — named Mel — is approximately ten months old. She cannot yet walk, but she is alert, responsive, and old enough to have a developing personality. Dante is stunned.

Emma tells Dante that Mel is his daughter. The timeline adds up: their relationship ended while Emma was pregnant, though she has kept this from him entirely. Dante had no knowledge of the pregnancy. He has missed the first ten months of his child's life — not through choice, but through deception.

Key Fact

Mel arrives in a pushchair and is approximately ten months old. She is not a newborn. Blackman chose this age deliberately: Mel is old enough to have needs and reactions, but young enough that Dante — who knows nothing about babies — finds her completely overwhelming.

The Deception and the Disappearance

Emma does not announce that she is leaving for good. Her method of abandonment is deceptive, and the deception is what makes it so devastating. She asks Dante to look after Mel while she pops out — the implication is that she will return. She does not return. Later, she sends a text message telling Dante that she will not be coming back.

There is no dramatic confrontation at the door, no tearful goodbye, no conversation about what happens next. Emma exits his life as quietly as possible, leaving Dante with Mel and no instruction, no preparation, and no support beyond his family. The casual brutality of a text message — not even a phone call — encapsulates Emma's refusal to take accountability.

Had Emma been honest about not wanting to return, Dante could have chosen how to respond. Instead she removes his agency. He is left in a situation not of his choosing, with a child he has known for one afternoon, unable to contact the mother, and unsure whether this is permanent. Blackman uses this to underline one of the novel's recurring themes: men can be the primary carers, whether they choose to be or not. Dante's journey into fatherhood begins not with a decision but with a deception.

Dante's First Response

Dante's initial reaction is shock. He does not immediately bond with Mel, nor does he immediately reject her. He is simply at a loss. He does not know how to hold her, how to soothe her, what she needs, or what he is supposed to do. The novel is honest about the learning curve: parenting is not instinctive for Dante. It is learned, slowly and sometimes painfully, over the course of the novel.

His father, Tyler — a widower who raised Dante and Adam alone after losing his wife to cancer — plays a crucial role in the early stages. Tyler's response to Mel is important: he does not condemn Dante. He accepts the situation and helps with the practicalities, modelling the same kind of stoic parental responsibility that has defined his own life. Blackman uses Tyler to show that single fatherhood is not extraordinary — it is what men in this family do.

Key Fact

The boys' mother died of cancer. Tyler has raised Dante and Adam as a widower. This is not an abandonment story — it is a family shaped by grief. Tyler's emotional guardedness stems from unprocessed loss, not bitterness at being left.

University Plans Collapse

Dante had planned to study journalism at university. This ambition is not vague — it is specific and carefully chosen. Within hours of receiving his results, that plan is in ruins. He cannot leave Mel with no one to care for her. He cannot go to university and take a baby. His academic achievement, the thing he has worked towards for two years, becomes meaningless in a single afternoon.

Blackman is deliberate about naming Dante's subject. Journalism is not a trivial aspiration — it is a career built on telling the truth, investigating the world, giving people a voice. The irony is that Dante is now silenced by his circumstances. His story, for the moment, is not one he can tell publicly. He is not the correspondent he wanted to become. He is a teenage father in his dad's house, learning to warm a bottle.

Critics have noted that Dante's career aspiration is meaningful within the novel's structure. Both boys are co-narrators — they tell their own stories in their own voices. In a sense, they are both already journalists of their own experience. Dante's voice is direct, practical, and observational. His frustrated dream becomes part of what he has to rebuild by the novel's end: a sense of a future that includes both Mel and the version of himself he was going to become.

The Dual-Narration Structure

Lesson 2 is also the right moment to consolidate understanding of Blackman's structural choice. The novel alternates between Dante's first-person chapters and Adam's first-person chapters. Each brother sees only his own crisis clearly; neither is fully aware of the other's. Dante is consumed by Mel. Adam is consumed by his own story — his relationship with Josh, his experiences at school, his sense of isolation.

The dual narration creates dramatic irony. We, as readers, see both boys struggling simultaneously. We understand the pressure building in the household before either brother fully articulates it. This technique also makes the novel's climax — when the two storylines violently converge — all the more powerful.
fields.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Dante plans to study journalism at university — a specific ambition that Blackman names deliberately.
  • Mel arrives in a pushchair at approximately ten months old; Emma's abandonment is deceptive — she leaves under the pretence of going out and texts later to say she will not return.
  • Tyler is a widower whose wife died of cancer; his steady response to the crisis models single fatherhood as something ordinary in this family, rooted in grief rather than abandonment.
  • The dual-narration structure gives readers simultaneous access to both brothers' crises, generating dramatic irony that builds towards the violent convergence of their storylines.
fields.exam_tip_html: For Edexcel, practise linking plot details to themes. When writing about Dante's story, make sure you can connect Emma's method of abandonment (the deception, the text message) to Blackman's theme of male responsibility thrust upon someone without choice. Examiners reward analysis that explains how a specific structural or narrative choice — like dual narration — creates meaning for the reader, not just what happens.

fields.description: Dante learns to care for Mel, navigates loss of his university plans, and the novel's theme of male nurturing.
fields.content_html:
The Demands of Real Fatherhood

Once Emma has gone and the reality of the situation becomes clear, Dante must simply get on with it. He has a baby daughter who is approximately ten months old, who cannot walk, who needs feeding, changing, comforting, and constant attention. He has no experience. He has no instruction manual. He has only his father Tyler — himself a man who raised two sons alone after the death of their mother — and whatever he can work out for himself.

Blackman presents the early stages of Dante's fatherhood without romanticisation. He is exhausted. He gets things wrong. He does not know how to read Mel's different cries. He does not know what she needs at two in the morning when she screams. The novel's portrait of parenting is specific and physical: nappies, milk, sleep deprivation, and the particular difficulty of managing a ten-month-old who is old enough to have strong preferences and reactions but too young to communicate them in words.

Key Fact

Mel is approximately ten months old. She arrived in a pushchair, not as a newborn. The specific demands Dante faces — a baby who is mobile, reactive, and demanding but unable to speak — are central to Blackman's portrait of involuntary fatherhood.

Sacrifice: What Dante Gives Up

The central sacrifice at the heart of Dante's storyline is his university place. He had worked towards studying journalism — a specific, carefully chosen ambition. A-level results day, which was supposed to be the beginning of his future, became the day his future was replaced by a different one.

Blackman takes care to show that Dante does not make this sacrifice quickly or easily. He wrestles with it. He considers possible routes — could he still go? Could someone else look after Mel? — before arriving at the reality that there is no adequate solution that does not involve him taking primary responsibility for his daughter's care. The journalism degree is not deferred. It is, for now, gone.

The sacrifice has symbolic weight. Journalism is about telling the truth, bearing witness, giving a voice to those who are not heard. Dante is now living a story he cannot yet tell. His sacrifice is not just material (the degree, the career) but also about identity: the version of himself he was going to become has been interrupted.

Part of what makes the novel's resolution satisfying is that Dante's sacrifice is not presented as permanent destruction. By the end, he has not recovered his journalism degree — but he has come to see Mel not as the thing that destroyed his future but as something integral to who he is. The novel does not pretend the sacrifice was easy or small. It does not resolve the loss. But it offers Dante a future that includes both Mel and a version of the self he was building before she arrived.

Tyler as a Model: The Widower Father

Tyler Bridgeman's parenting is the template Dante has grown up with. Tyler is a widower: his wife — the boys' mother — died of cancer. He raised Dante and Adam alone, not because he was abandoned or because a partnership broke down, but because he was bereaved. His emotional landscape has been shaped by grief that he has never fully processed. He is stoic, practical, and present — but not emotionally expressive. He provides. He does not open up.

When Mel arrives, Tyler's response is instructive. He does not condemn Dante. He does not perform shock or outrage. He assesses the practical reality and helps. This is the only mode of fatherhood he knows: stoic acceptance and practical action. For Dante, Tyler's model is both a gift and a limitation. It gives him a foundation — he has seen what it looks like for a man to take full parental responsibility without complaint. But it does not give him a template for emotional expressiveness or vulnerability.

Key Fact

The boys' mother died of cancer. Tyler is a widower, not a man whose partner left him. His emotional guardedness is rooted in unprocessed grief — a man who has buried loss under duty and practicality. His parenting is an act of love expressed through action rather than words.

Blackman's Argument About Masculinity

The novel's title — Boys Don't Cry — is a phrase used to police male emotional expression. Boys are told, from childhood, that vulnerability is weakness, that tears are failure, that masculinity means stoicism and endurance. The novel challenges this at every level.

Dante's journey into fatherhood is partly a journey into the emotional life he has been taught to suppress. Caring for Mel requires him to be attentive, patient, and emotionally present in ways that the traditional male scripts around him do not support. He cannot be stoic with a ten-month-old who needs comfort. He must actually show up emotionally. This is Blackman's central argument: the capacity to nurture is not gendered. Boys can cry. Men can care.

Both brothers are, in different ways, under pressure to conform to a version of masculinity that does not fit them. Dante is expected to be free of parental responsibility at seventeen — fatherhood is not in the script. Adam is expected to be heterosexual — his sexuality is not in the script. Both are living outside the expectations placed on them as young men. Blackman uses the dual-narration structure to show these pressures operating simultaneously, and the climax — when the two storylines converge in violence — is the moment at which the pressure of social expectation becomes literally lethal.

Growing into Fatherhood

Over the course of the novel, Dante's relationship with Mel changes. The initial shock and helplessness give way, slowly, to competence. He learns what she needs. He learns her patterns. He learns to read her differently at different times of day. And with competence comes something else: attachment.

Mel is not an obstacle in Dante's story. She is not something he merely tolerates while waiting for his real life to begin. Blackman charts the transition from Dante caring for Mel because he has no choice to Dante caring for Mel because he loves her. This transition is the emotional spine of his storyline — and by the novel's end, it is clear that whatever future Dante builds, Mel is part of it.
fields.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Dante's sacrifice is specific: he gives up a planned journalism degree to care for Mel, who is approximately ten months old and arrived in a pushchair.
  • Tyler models stoic, practical fatherhood rooted in grief — he is a widower whose wife died of cancer, not a man whose partner left him.
  • The title 'Boys Don't Cry' is a social script that the novel systematically dismantles — Dante's journey into fatherhood requires emotional presence, not stoicism.
  • Both brothers are under pressure to conform to masculine expectations that do not fit them — the dual narration shows these pressures operating simultaneously.
fields.exam_tip_html: When writing about the theme of fatherhood, make sure you demonstrate awareness of Blackman's specific choices: Dante plans to study journalism (not a generic university course), Mel is approximately ten months old (not a newborn), and Tyler is a widower (not an abandoned partner). These specific details matter to examiners. They also signal that you have read carefully rather than relying on a generic overview.

fields.content_html:
The Evening of the Attack

The novel's most violent and pivotal sequence takes place at a party following a celebration at the Bar Belle pub — an event connected to Dante's eighteenth birthday. The two storylines that have been running in parallel throughout the novel — Dante's fatherhood and Adam's secret relationship — are brought together at this party. Adam is present. Josh is present. Logan and Paul are present. The scene is set for a catastrophic collision.

Earlier in the evening, Adam is outed in front of the group. This exposure is the trigger for what follows. The information lands badly in this environment — a social world built on masculine conformity, where homophobia has been casual and unchallenged.

The Attackers: Josh, Logan, and Paul

The attack on Adam is carried out by three people: Josh, Logan, and Paul. All three are Dante's friends. This fact — that Adam's attackers are people Dante has trusted — is central to the novel's emotional and thematic force.

The specific roles are equally important. Josh — Adam's own secret boyfriend — is the one who beats Adam. Logan and Paul physically restrain Dante, preventing him from intervening. Josh does not stand back. He does not hesitate. He attacks the person he has been intimate with.

Key Fact

The attackers are Josh, Logan, and Paul — all Dante's friends. Josh, Adam's former secret boyfriend, is the one who beats Adam. Logan and Paul hold Dante back. The attack is a direct product of internalised homophobia: Josh attacks the person he has been with in order to prove, to Logan and to himself, that he is not gay.

Logan's Engineering: A Test of Masculinity

The attack is not spontaneous. It is later revealed that Logan engineered the situation as a test. Logan knows — or suspects — that Josh has been involved with Adam. He uses the moment of Adam being outed to corner Josh: prove you are not gay, or be outed yourself. The logic of the test is the logic of peer pressure taken to its most violent extreme.

Josh does not resist. He is not strong enough — not yet — to withstand the pressure. He chooses violence over vulnerability. In attacking Adam, he attacks the version of himself he cannot accept. Blackman makes this psychologically coherent: Josh's violence is the product of shame, not of hatred in its simplest form. He is not a monster. He is a person who has been broken by the social world he lives in — and who, in his breaking, breaks someone else catastrophically.

The fact that Adam's attacker is his own boyfriend — the person who, in a different world, should be his protector — is the novel's most powerful irony. Blackman constructs this carefully. Josh and Adam's relationship has been built on secrecy and Josh's shame. The attack is the logical endpoint of that shame: Josh, given a social test, chooses violence over honesty. The relationship that Adam hoped might contain connection instead contains the instrument of his hospitalisation. This is what internalised homophobia destroys.

Adam Hospitalised

The attack leaves Adam in critical condition. He is not taken home. He does not recover at the kitchen table. Adam is hospitalised. The severity of the attack is conveyed through the gravity of his medical status: this was not a scuffle. This was a serious, sustained assault.

Dante, after being restrained and unable to stop the attack, reports to the police what happened. He names the attackers. This is an act of moral clarity in a moment of devastation: Dante does not protect his friends by staying silent. He tells the truth — which is, perhaps, the closest he comes in this moment to the journalist he planned to be.

Key Fact

Adam is hospitalised in critical condition. Dante reports to the police what happened and names the attackers. Adam does not go home after the attack. His recovery takes place after his hospitalisation, during which he withdraws, becomes depressed, and eventually faces a suicidal crisis before recovering.

Adam's Recovery: Depression and Withdrawal

After his discharge from hospital, Adam withdraws. He does not bounce back. He stays in his room. He barely communicates. He becomes depressed. The novel does not skip from the attack to recovery. It insists on the reality that violence of this kind has lasting consequences. Adam's mental health deteriorates to the point of a suicidal crisis.

Blackman handles this section with considerable care. Adam's depression is not presented as weakness. It is a rational response to being severely beaten by someone he trusted, in a public setting, while the people he might have looked to for protection were unable to help him. His withdrawal is a form of protection, a body and mind recoiling from a world that has shown itself to be dangerous.

Blackman's choice to show Adam's depression and withdrawal in full is part of the novel's commitment to honesty. A version of this story could have shown Adam attacked and then resilient — a triumph-over-adversity narrative. Instead, Blackman insists on the full cost: hospitalisation, depression, withdrawal, suicidal ideation. This is the real shape of trauma recovery. It is also part of the novel's argument: the violence is not just a bad night. It has consequences that last.

Josh's Confession and Accountability

Eventually, Josh's own story catches up with him. He kisses Dante — revealing to Dante that he is gay himself. He apologises to Adam, unreservedly. And he turns himself in to the police. This does not undo what he did. It does not restore what was taken from Adam. But it is the closest the novel comes to showing the human capacity for accountability among those who have caused harm.

Josh's arc is a tragedy of internalised homophobia: a person who had the capacity for love but was destroyed by shame, who destroyed someone else before finding the courage to be honest. His eventual honesty is not redemption in the full sense — Blackman is too precise for that — but it is an acknowledgement of truth.

Resolution: Resilience and Acceptance

The novel's resolution refuses simple happiness. Adam recovers — physically and, over time, emotionally. He does not become the person he was before the attack. But he survives. Dante, in parallel, has grown into his relationship with Mel. The family, including Tyler, has been brought to a point of greater openness. The reconciliation is hard-won and real.

Blackman ends the novel with Dante embracing fatherhood rather than enduring it, and Adam facing a future rather than being defined by his ordeal. Neither resolution is easy or uncomplicated. But both are earned — through suffering, growth, and the particular resilience that the novel argues is available to people who refuse to let shame govern their lives.

Dante Bridgeman

Dante is the novel's primary protagonist and one of its two co-narrators. At seventeen, he is defined by ambition, intelligence, and a specific goal: studying journalism at university. His chapters are characterised by a direct, observational voice — practical, outward-looking, focused on the world he is trying to navigate. Journalism, for Dante, is not just a career. It is a vocation built on truth-telling and bearing witness. Blackman names this aspiration deliberately.

Dante's crisis is visible and external: a baby arrives, a university place is lost, a life plan is overturned in an afternoon. But the novel is equally interested in what this external disruption does to his sense of self. Dante is not simply coping with a practical problem. He is confronting the gap between the person he was becoming and the person his circumstances now require him to be. His journey is about finding a way to hold both.

By the novel's end, Dante has grown into fatherhood rather than merely enduring it. He has also demonstrated moral courage when it matters most: he names his own friends — people he trusted — as Adam's attackers and reports them to the police. This act connects him, symbolically, to the journalist he wanted to become: a person who tells the truth regardless of the social cost.

Key Fact

Dante plans to study journalism. He loses this plan when Mel arrives. At the novel's climax, he reports his own friends to the police — an act of truth-telling that echoes the journalist he was going to be.

Adam Bridgeman

Adam is Dante's sixteen-year-old younger brother and the novel's second narrator. From the opening pages, Adam is openly gay. He has known since he was thirteen and, in his own words, he likes it. He is not hiding who he is. He is not in the process of coming out. He is already out — and the world, in its cruelty, has noticed.

Adam is bullied at school specifically because he is openly gay. His challenge throughout the novel is not concealment but survival: navigating a social environment that punishes him for his openness. His voice in the novel is equally precise and honest as Dante's — but where Dante looks outward, Adam is more often engaged with the interior life, with feeling and meaning and connection.

After the attack, Adam withdraws. He does not immediately recover. He becomes depressed, retreats to his room, and faces a suicidal crisis before eventually recovering. Blackman insists on the full aftermath of trauma. Adam's resilience is not effortless. It is the result of surviving something that nearly destroyed him.

Key Fact

Adam is openly gay from the novel's opening. He is targeted because he refuses to hide who he is. After the attack, he is hospitalised, then withdraws into depression. His eventual recovery is hard-won, not automatic.

Tyler Bridgeman (Dad)

Tyler is a single father — but not because he was left by a partner. His wife, the boys' mother, died of cancer. Tyler has raised Dante and Adam as a widower. This is one of the novel's most important factual details, because the nature of his loss entirely determines the nature of his characterisation.

Tyler's emotional guardedness — his inability to express vulnerability, his tendency to show love through action rather than words — is rooted in unprocessed grief. He is not a bitter man who was abandoned. He is a man who buried a devastating loss under stoicism and practicality and never dug it back out. He provided. He showed up. He kept the family functioning. But he did not open up. He did not cry. He modelled the very script the novel's title challenges: boys don't cry.

Tyler's response to the two crises — Mel's arrival and the attack on Adam — is consistent with this characterisation. He does not perform shock or condemnation. He assesses, accepts, and helps. He is not the warmest father imaginable, but he is present and reliable. For Dante and Adam, this is foundational: a father who stayed.

Tyler's inability to express grief has a direct effect on his sons. Dante and Adam have grown up in a household where loss is not spoken about, where vulnerability is managed through action. This shapes both of them. Dante's instinct, when faced with crisis, is to get on with it — Tyler's model. Adam's interior life, by contrast, is richly emotional and expressive, which sets him at odds with the masculine norms of his environment. Both are shaped by a father doing his best under the pressure of grief he has never processed.

Josh

Josh is one of Dante's friends and Adam's secret boyfriend — but these facts must be understood in the context of what Josh actually does and represents in the novel. Josh is not a sympathetic romantic figure. He is one of the most psychologically complex and morally troubling characters Blackman creates.

Josh is deeply closeted and consumed by shame about his own sexuality. He insists that his relationship with Adam remain completely hidden. He demands secrecy. He is not comfortable with Adam being gay; he is not comfortable with himself being gay. The relationship does not offer Adam a haven of acceptance. It offers a connection built on Josh's self-loathing and the constant pressure of secrecy.

At the novel's climax, Josh participates in the homophobic attack on Adam. He is the one who beats Adam, while Logan and Paul restrain Dante. The context is revealing: Logan engineers the attack as a test — Josh must prove to the group that he is not gay. Josh, unable to withstand the pressure, chooses violence. He attacks the person he has been intimate with in order to protect his own public identity.

Later, Josh confesses to Dante (revealing his own sexuality), apologises unreservedly to Adam, and turns himself in to the police. His arc is not one of acceptance and love — it is the arc of a person destroyed by internalised homophobia who eventually finds the courage to be honest about what he has done and what he is. He is not a villain in a simple sense, but he causes devastating harm.

Key Fact

Josh is not a symbol of acceptance. He is Adam's secret boyfriend and one of his attackers — a character whose arc demonstrates the destruction caused by internalised homophobia and shame. His eventual accountability does not erase the harm he caused.

Logan and Paul

Logan and Paul are Dante's other friends who participate in the attack. Logan engineers the assault — it is his decision to use Adam's outing as a test for Josh. Paul is a participant in the restraint of Dante. Both represent the wider social complicity that makes the attack possible: a friend group in which homophobia is casual, unchallenged, and, at Logan's instigation, weaponised.

Aunt Jackie

Aunt Jackie is a supporting character who provides emotional warmth and practical support that Tyler cannot always offer. She is not a central figure, but her presence signals that the Bridgeman family is not entirely isolated in its crises. She represents the extended family as a resource — people who show up without condemnation.

Emma Bryce

Emma is Dante's ex-girlfriend and Mel's mother. She appears briefly — arriving with Mel in a pushchair and then disappearing, never to return. She communicates her decision not to return via text message. Emma is largely absent from the novel after this point, but her absence is significant. She represents a form of irresponsibility that the novel uses to put Dante's eventual responsibility into sharper relief. The contrast between Emma, who leaves, and Dante, who stays, is a central structural device.

In your exam response, always move from identifying a technique to explaining its effect on the audience and then connecting it to a wider theme. For example: state what the playwright does, explain how they do it using precise language, and argue what this reveals about character, theme, or context. This three-step approach — what, how, why — will take your analysis to the top band.
fields.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Dante: aspired to study journalism; loses his university plans to care for Mel; grows into fatherhood and demonstrates moral courage by naming his friends as Adam's attackers.
  • Adam: openly gay from the novel's opening; faces bullying because he refuses to hide; is hospitalised after the attack, then withdraws into depression before recovering.
  • Tyler: the boys' mother died of cancer — he is a widower, not an abandoned partner; his emotional guardedness stems from unprocessed grief.
  • Josh: Adam's secret boyfriend and the person who beats him in the attack; deeply closeted and consumed by internalised homophobia; later confesses, apologises, and turns himself in — accountability, not redemption.

fields.exam_tip_html: Character analysis questions in Edexcel often ask about a single character across the whole novel. For Josh, be clear that he is not a positive character — his role is to explore internalised homophobia, and his arc leads to violence before it reaches accountability. For Tyler, be precise: his wife died of cancer (not left), and his emotional limitations are rooted in grief. For Adam, emphasise that he is openly gay from the start — his challenge is survival, not concealment.

fields.content_html:
The Novel's Central Themes

Boys Don't Cry is a novel about the cost of conformity — what happens to individuals and families when social expectations override honesty, vulnerability, and love. Blackman develops this argument through four interlocking themes: masculinity and emotional repression; homophobia and its consequences; fatherhood and responsibility; and the family as a site of both damage and recovery.

Theme 1: Masculinity and Emotional Repression

The title is the novel's thesis statement. Boys Don't Cry is a cultural instruction — a script handed to young men telling them that vulnerability is weakness, that stoicism is strength, that emotion must be suppressed. Blackman uses every major male character to interrogate this script.

Tyler represents the cost of compliance. He has buried grief — his wife died of cancer — under decades of practical, stoic parenting. He loves his sons. He has never told them in a way they can hear. His model of fatherhood produces reliable, practical men who do not know how to express what they feel.

Dante begins the novel in the grip of this script and ends by breaking it. Caring for Mel forces him to be emotionally present in ways the masculine script does not support. His growth is measured by his increasing willingness to feel — to be attached, to be frightened, to love without reservation.

Josh represents the most destructive endpoint of emotional repression: a person who cannot acknowledge his own identity and, in the act of repressing it, turns violent. His attack on Adam is not incidental to his psychological state. It is produced by it. Josh's violence is the product of shame and suppression taken to their logical extreme.

Key Fact

'Boys Don't Cry' is not just a title — it is the novel's central argument. Blackman uses it to name the social script that damages every male character in the book, from Tyler's buried grief to Josh's violent suppression of his own identity.

Theme 2: Homophobia and Internalised Homophobia

The novel presents two faces of homophobia: external and internalised. Adam faces external homophobia: he is openly gay, and he is bullied and ultimately violently attacked because of it. The external hostility is real, sustained, and dangerous. But Blackman argues that internalised homophobia — the kind Josh carries — is equally destructive, and perhaps more so, because it destroys from within.

Josh's arc is the novel's most powerful exploration of what shame does to a person. He knows he is gay. He cannot accept it. He insists on concealment, builds a secret relationship on a foundation of self-loathing, and when that self-loathing is tested under social pressure — Logan's engineered test of masculinity — he responds with violence. He attacks the person he has been intimate with in order to protect his own public identity. This is not random cruelty. It is the logical endpoint of shame left unaddressed.

The contrast between Adam and Josh is structurally central. Adam's openness is not naivety — he knows what it costs. But his openness does not destroy him. Josh's concealment does destroy him, and nearly destroys Adam in the process. Blackman's argument is not that openness is safe. It is that concealment is lethal.

Logan's role is to engineer the conditions for the attack. He is not a mindless bigot — he is a strategist. He identifies Josh's vulnerability (his concealed sexuality) and uses it as a lever. His test — 'prove you're not gay' — is the mechanism by which peer pressure becomes hate crime. Logan represents the social infrastructure of homophobia: the culture in which violence is organised and normalised. Paul's participation in restraining Dante makes him complicit in the same logic. Blackman uses these characters to show that the attack is not an aberration — it is the product of a social world that has been building towards it.

Theme 3: Fatherhood and Responsibility

Fatherhood is presented as a choice — not a biological given. Tyler chose to stay and raise his sons after his wife died. Dante is thrust into fatherhood without choice, but the novel charts his decision to embrace it rather than escape it. Emma chose to leave. The contrast is deliberate.

Blackman challenges the assumption that fatherhood is a secondary or optional role for men. She presents three generations of Bridgeman men — Tyler, Dante, and, prospectively, the version of Dante who will one day explain himself to Mel — and uses all of them to argue that the capacity to nurture is not gendered. Men can be primary carers. They can love children in the full, expressive, emotionally present way that the masculine script tells them not to. Dante's growth is into this kind of love.

Emma Bryce is used as a structural counterpoint. Her choice to leave — communicated by a text message — throws Dante's eventual choice to stay into sharper relief. Blackman does not develop Emma as a character with her own complexity. She is present to make Dante's responsibility more visible.

Key Fact

The boys' mother died of cancer. Tyler is a widower who raised his sons through grief. His emotional guardedness comes from buried loss, not bitterness at being left. This distinction shapes the entire characterisation of his parenting.

Theme 4: Family, Damage, and Recovery

The Bridgeman family is a family shaped by loss — the death of a mother, the suppression of grief, the absence of emotional vocabulary. Into this family comes Mel, and then the violence done to Adam. Both events crack the family open in ways that, eventually, allow something to change.

The novel does not offer a resolution in which the family is healed and made whole. It offers something more realistic: a family that has moved, slightly, towards openness. Dante has grown into something Tyler could not be. Adam has survived something that nearly killed him. Tyler has been present for both crises without running away. The family is still limited, still shaped by grief and habit. But it is, by the end, a family that has been tested and has held.

Blackman's Craft: Narrative Technique

The novel's most important structural choice is its dual narration. Dante and Adam alternate chapters. Each tells his own story. Neither has full access to the other's experience — but the reader does. This creates dramatic irony at the macro level: we watch two crises building towards each other, aware of the full picture in a way that neither brother is.

The technique also forces the reader to hold two experiences simultaneously. Dante's practical, outward-looking voice and Adam's more interior, emotionally attentive voice represent two ways of inhabiting the world — and Blackman suggests that both are necessary. Neither brother alone gives the full picture. Together, they do.

The novel was published in 2010, three years before Blackman became Children's Laureate (2013–2015). Her choice to write about teenage fatherhood and homophobic violence — in a novel aimed at young adult readers — reflects her consistent commitment to writing stories that young people actually need, about things that actually happen to them.

Exam Technique: Writing About Boys Don't Cry

Edexcel English Literature requires you to write about the whole novel in response to a question built around a short quotation. Here are the key principles:

Even if the quotation is from early in the novel, your response must range across the whole text. A character who appears minor in the opening chapters may be crucial later. Josh is introduced as a friend of Dante's; by the climax he is the person who hospitalises Adam. This arc must be understood as a whole if you are to write convincingly about him.

Examiners are alert to basic factual errors. Key facts to have correct: Dante plans to study journalism; Mel is approximately ten months old, arriving in a pushchair; the boys' mother died of cancer (not left); Josh, Logan, and Paul are the attackers, with Josh beating Adam; Adam is hospitalised (not taken home); Josh later turns himself in to the police. These specific details distinguish a well-read student from one working from memory alone.

The Edexcel mark scheme rewards analysis that moves between language and theme. This means: identify what is said (the quotation), explore how it is said (Blackman's language choices, narrative technique, structure), and explain what it means thematically (what idea about masculinity, homophobia, responsibility, or family is being developed). A response that identifies technique without connecting it to meaning, or identifies theme without grounding it in language, will be limited to the middle bands.

fields.content_html:
Theme 1: Truth and Deception

The most pervasive theme in Stephens's play is the tension between Christopher's absolute commitment to truth and the adults around him who deceive him in the name of love. 'I do not tell lies' is Christopher's defining principle — yet he lives in a world constructed almost entirely from lies. Ed lied about Judy dying. Ed lied about killing Wellington. The entire domestic reality of Act 1 is a fiction.

Stephens presents this tension without simple moral resolution. Ed's lies are motivated by love, not malice. He believed — wrongly — that his version of reality would protect Christopher from pain. The play shows that this kind of protective deception is ultimately more harmful than the truth would have been: Christopher's response to learning his father has lied is not grief but logical deduction that his father might harm him. The architecture of lies collapses into danger rather than safety.

Key Fact

The central irony: Ed lies to protect Christopher, but because Christopher values truth absolutely ('I do not tell lies'), the discovery of the lies is uniquely destructive — more damaging than the truth would have been. Love expressed through deception becomes a form of harm.

Theme 2: Family, Trust, and Broken Relationships

The play presents a family that has failed in multiple directions simultaneously. Ed's marriage collapsed; Judy left Christopher and moved to London; Ed rebuilt a partial relationship with Mrs Shears which also collapsed. Christopher exists at the centre of these adult failures, protected from them by lies but shaped by the absences they create.

Stephens does not present family restoration as straightforwardly possible. At the end of the play, Christopher has shared custody between Ed and Judy. This is not the recovery of a nuclear family but a functional arrangement that acknowledges what has broken and what remains. The play's treatment of family is honest and uncomfortable: love is real, damage is real, and both persist simultaneously.

Christopher's relationships with Ed and Judy are both complex and asymmetric. Ed is consistently present — even when he lies, he is there, managing, protecting, doing what he can. Judy is absent, then suddenly present, overwhelmed by guilt. Both relationships are shaped by Christopher's additional needs: Ed's deception partly reflects the exhaustion of single parenting; Judy's departure partly reflects the difficulty of that same challenge. Stephens presents both parents as struggling with something genuinely hard, rather than condemning either of them. The play asks the audience to hold complexity: to see the damage and the love at once.

Theme 3: Independence and Bravery

Christopher's journey to London is the play's central act of bravery. He has never travelled independently. The journey subjects him to everything he finds most difficult — crowds, unpredictability, sensory overload — and he survives it, finds his mother, and returns. The theatrical staging of the journey (Frantic Assembly's choreography, the ensemble as crowd) makes the scale of this achievement physically present for the audience.

The play frames bravery in Christopher's own terms. He does not experience the journey as heroic — he experiences it as terrifying. But he does it anyway, step by step, because the logic of his situation demands it. His bravery is not the instinctive courage of a conventional protagonist; it is the determined, methodical persistence of a person who continues because the alternative — not knowing — is worse. This is a distinctive form of bravery that the play invites the audience to recognise and admire.

Key Fact

Christopher's bravery is methodical and determined rather than instinctive. He does not feel brave — he feels terrified. But he continues because the logic of his situation demands it. The play invites the audience to recognise this as a form of courage that neurotypical frameworks often miss.

Theme 4: Neurodiversity and the Challenge to the Deficit Model

Stephens's play consistently presents Christopher's neurodivergent way of experiencing the world as the audience's primary reality. His literal language, his logical deduction, his mathematical precision, his need for predictable routine — these are not presented as limitations to be overcome but as characteristics that produce both exceptional capability and genuine vulnerability. The play challenges the audience to recognise that the neurotypical world — its ambiguity, its use of social lies, its non-verbal codes — is just as difficult and arbitrary as it feels to Christopher.

For AO4 (context), students should engage with the theatrical and cultural context of the 2012 National Theatre premiere. Writing for a 2012 audience, adapting a 2003 novel, Stephens continued Haddon's challenge to the deficit model of autism. The play-within-a-play structure, in which the audience inhabits Christopher's perspective throughout, is a theatrical embodiment of this challenge: the audience sees the world as Christopher does, not as the neurotypical adults do.

Key Quotations for the Eduqas Exam

The following quotations are reliably attested in the play-text and are appropriate for the Eduqas exam. All are framed as play quotations, not novel quotations:

'I do not tell lies.' — Christopher's core principle. Use to analyse his character's relationship to truth and why deception is uniquely damaging to him.

'I find people confusing.' — Christopher's explanation of his social difficulties. Use to analyse his relationship to language and communication.

'I am not a very good mother, Christopher. Maybe if things had been different... maybe if you'd been different... but that is not your fault.' — Judy's letter. Use to analyse Judy's character, the theme of parental failure, and the complexity of responsibility.

'Prime numbers are what is left when you have taken all the patterns away.' — Christopher on mathematics. Use to analyse his relationship to certainty and the symbolism of mathematics.

'Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?' — The play's final question. Use to analyse the ending, the question vs declaration distinction, and Siobhan's significance as the person whose answer matters most.

'Siobhan understands. When she tells me not to do something she tells me exactly what it is I am not allowed to do. I like this.' — Christopher on Siobhan. Use to analyse his relationship with her and the theme of clear communication.

Key Fact

Core play quotations: 'I do not tell lies' (truth/character); 'I find people confusing' (communication); 'that is not your fault' (family/Judy); 'Prime numbers... patterns away' (mathematics/certainty); 'Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?' (ending/independence); Siobhan understands (trust/communication).

Exam Technique: Writing About a Play

The your written exam question gives you a short extract from the play and asks you to analyse it and the play as a whole. The question is worth 40 marks (35 for quality + 5 for accuracy and ambition in spelling, punctuation, and vocabulary).

A strong response will: attribute craft choices to 'Stephens' not 'Haddon'; analyse theatrical devices as well as language; embed AO4 context naturally (2012 National Theatre premiere, the challenge to the deficit model, Stephens's adaptation of Haddon); range across the whole play; and use precisely worded quotations from the play-text.

For AO4, include context about the play, not just the novel. Useful AO4 points include: Stephens's 2012 adaptation for the National Theatre, directed by Marianne Elliott; the production's use of Frantic Assembly's physical theatre to embody Christopher's sensory experience; the seven Olivier Awards and five Tony Awards (indicating the play's cultural significance and reach); the challenge to the deficit model of autism in both 2003 (Haddon's novel) and 2012 (Stephens's play). The novel's Whitbread Award is useful background context, but it is the play's theatrical context that is directly relevant for AO4 in the Eduqas exam.

Example AO4 sentence: 'Adapting Haddon's 2003 novel for the National Theatre in 2012, Stephens uses Siobhan's co-narration to present Christopher's perspective directly to the audience, challenging the deficit model of autism by making Christopher's logical and mathematical way of experiencing the world the primary lens through which the audience understands events.'

Model Analytical Paragraph

Here is a model paragraph demonstrating how to write about the Stephens play at a high level:

'Stephens presents Christopher's relationship with truth as both his greatest strength and his greatest vulnerability. His declaration 'I do not tell lies' establishes an absolute moral standard that the play's adult world consistently fails to meet, creating a sustained dramatic irony in which the audience comes to recognise Christopher's truthfulness as more ethically consistent than the neurotypical deceptions that surround him. The theatrical effect of the play-within-a-play structure is to align the audience with Christopher's perspective: as Siobhan reads his account, we understand what the adults do not. When Ed's lies are revealed in Act 2, Christopher's logical deduction — that if Father has lied, Father might harm him — is presented not as a symptom of his neurodivergence but as a rational response to available evidence. Stephens uses Christopher's literal logic to expose the self-deception in Ed's protective dishonesty, suggesting that love without honesty is ultimately a form of harm.'

Effective drama analysis requires attention to stagecraft — considering not just what happens but how the playwright shapes the audience's response through every element of performance and text. In your exam response, identify specific techniques and explain their effect precisely.

fields.exam_tip_html: In the Eduqas exam, always write 'Stephens presents' not 'Haddon presents'. Never mention chapters — use 'the play', 'Act 1', 'Act 2', 'the scene'. Always refer to the play's ending correctly: Christopher asks Siobhan 'Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?' — a question, not the novel's declarative 'I can do anything'. When embedding AO4 context, prioritise the 2012 theatrical context (National Theatre premiere, Frantic Assembly, Olivier/Tony Awards) alongside the novel's 2003 background.
fields.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The central irony of the truth/deception theme: Ed's protective lies are more harmful than the truth would have been, because Christopher's literal commitment to honesty makes deception uniquely destructive.
  • The play ends with Christopher asking Siobhan a question ('Does that mean I can do anything?') — not the novel's declaration. This is the most important single distinction for the Eduqas exam.
  • AO4 context must reference the play: 2012 National Theatre premiere, Marianne Elliott, Frantic Assembly, seven Olivier Awards, Stephens's adaptation choices.

knowledge_checks.q: What is the central irony of the truth/deception theme?
options: Christopher lies to protect his father, but Ed discovers the truth anyway
Judy is honest but Christopher doesn't believe her
Ed's protective lies are more harmful than the truth would have been, because Christopher values truth absolutely
The detective investigation reveals that Christopher is the real cause of the family's problems

knowledge_checks.q: Which quotation correctly represents the play's ending — not the novel's?
options: 'And that means I can do anything.'
'Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?'
'I know I can do this because I went to London on my own.'
'I solved the mystery of Who Killed Wellington?'

knowledge_checks.q: Christopher says: 'I do not tell _____.' — his defining moral principle.
For AO4 in the Eduqas exam, students should prioritise the _____ context of Stephens's 2012 play, not just Haddon's 2003 novel.
Match each key quotation to its thematic relevance:
left: 'Prime numbers are what is left when you have taken all the patterns away'
'Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?'
right: Truth and deception — Christopher's absolute commitment to honesty makes Ed's lies uniquely damaging
Mathematics and certainty — Christopher's language of clarity and precision in an ambiguous world
Independence and the ending — aspiration rather than certainty, directed to the one person Christopher trusts

glossary_terms.definition: A model that views neurological difference as a disorder requiring correction — the play challenges this by presenting Christopher's logical way of experiencing the world as the audience's primary reality.

Assessment Objective 4 — showing understanding of the relationships between texts and the contexts in which they were written, performed, and received. For this play, AO4 should reference the 2012 theatrical context.
When the audience knows something a character does not — the play generates dramatic irony by showing the audience, through Siobhan's narration, what Christopher understands and what he misses.

The development of a theme through the course of the play — the truth/deception theme arcs from Act 1 (the lies in place) through Act 2 (the collapse of the lies) to the ending (what remains after the truth).
A sentence that asks a question — the form of the play's final line, distinguishing it from the novel's declarative certainty and creating an open, aspirational ending.
The playwright's use of dramatic techniques including staging, lighting, dialogue, and structure to create meaning.
The sense of anticipation or unease created by conflict, uncertainty, or approaching crisis in drama.

practice_questions.text: How does Stephens present the theme of truth and deception in the play?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of the central irony: Ed's protective deception is uniquely harmful to Christopher because of his absolute commitment to truth. Discusses: 'I do not tell lies', the interconnected web of Ed's lies, Christopher's logical response to the confession, Judy's letters and her admission ('I am not a very good mother... that is not your fault'), Siobhan's contrasting honesty. Range across both acts.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis with sustained evidence.
Mid band (15-21): Explained response engaging with the theme.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Some relevant points.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Stephens explore the theme of family in the play?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of the play's complex treatment of family. Discusses: Ed's love and deception as simultaneous, Judy's absence and guilt ('I am not a very good mother'), the discovery of the letters as the moment the false family is exposed, the shared custody as honest rather than restored resolution. AO4: challenges of family under pressure; single parenting of a child with additional needs.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis with range.
Mid band (15-21): Explained response.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Some points.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Stephens present independence and bravery through Christopher's journey in the play?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of Christopher's distinctive bravery: methodical, terrified, determined. Discusses the theatrical staging of the journey (ensemble as sensory overload), Toby's rescue, the arrival in London, and the connection between the journey and the final question ('Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?'). What does the play suggest about bravery for a neurodivergent person?
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis with theatrical awareness.
Mid band (15-21): Explained response.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Some points.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Stephens use the play to challenge attitudes towards neurodiversity?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of how the play's form embeds the challenge to the deficit model. Discusses: the play-within-a-play making Christopher's perspective the audience's primary reality, his literal logic as morally consistent, his mathematical precision as a form of excellence, and the way the neurotypical world (ambiguity, lies, non-verbal codes) is presented as strange from Christopher's viewpoint. AO4: 2012 theatrical context, neurodiversity discourse.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis with AO4 embedded.
Mid band (15-21): Explained response.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Some points.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Stephens use Siobhan's final role in the play to bring together the themes of trust, communication, and independence?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of the final scene as convergence of themes. Siobhan's trustworthiness (established through precise communication throughout) makes her the right person for Christopher to ask his final question. Her co-narrator role means she has been present at every moment of the play — she has witnessed everything. Christopher asking her 'Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?' brings together the trust theme (who can Christopher rely on?), the communication theme (who communicates honestly with him?), and the independence theme (what has he proved about himself?).
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis with range.
Mid band (15-21): Explained response.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Some points.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Stephens present the ending of the play as both hopeful and uncertain?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of the ending's tonal complexity. Hopeful: the A* result, the question to Siobhan, the tentative reconciliation with Ed, the gift of Sandy. Uncertain: the question is unanswered, the family is not restored, the relationship with Ed requires rebuilding. Discusses the question form as theatrically open (contrasts with the novel's declarative certainty). AO2: what the question vs declaration distinction means for meaning and audience response.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis of both tones.
Mid band (15-21): Some engagement with complexity.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Basic points.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

fields.content_html:
The Core Themes

A Christmas Carol braids together several interlocking themes. The most important are redemption, social responsibility, family, isolation, poverty, and the Christmas spirit. Thinking of these as a thematic web rather than a list means you can always move from one to another: Scrooge’s isolation is caused by greed, cured by memory, and transformed into family warmth. Good answers draw threads between themes, not walls around them.

Key Fact

The six key themes are: redemption, social responsibility, family, isolation, poverty and the spirit of Christmas. Colour-coding quotations by theme in your notebook is the fastest way to build a revision bank for the extract essay.

Redemption

Redemption is the novella’s structural backbone. Dickens shows it as a three-stage process: confrontation with the past (Stave 2), recognition of present harm (Stave 3), and fear of future consequence (Stave 4). The pattern echoes the Christian conversion narratives familiar to Victorian readers. Useful quotations: “I will honour Christmas in my heart”; “I am not the man I was.”

Social Responsibility and Poverty

Dickens wrote the novella in 1843, the year after the Second Report of the Children’s Employment Commission revealed the scale of child labour in Britain. The children Ignorance and Want are Dickens’s strongest argument that the middle and upper classes must engage with poverty. Link this theme to Scrooge’s “decrease the surplus population” (echoing Malthus), Marley’s “Mankind was my business”, and the Ghost of Christmas Present’s warning about Tim: “the child will die.”

Family appears through the Cratchits, Fred’s party and Belle’s later household. Each scene is a counterexample to Scrooge’s chosen isolation. Useful quotations: “God bless us, every one!” (Tiny Tim) and “my dear” (Mrs Cratchit, even in the face of Scrooge’s name).

Isolation is expressed through the adjective “solitary”, applied to Scrooge as a schoolboy and later as an adult. Dickens makes loneliness a self-imposed penalty: “as solitary as an oyster.” The Christmas spirit — “a kind, forgiving, charitable, pleasant time” (Fred) — is the antidote.

Reading the Extract Question

OCR gives you an extract plus a question asking you to start with the extract and then explore the whole novella. The command is clear: you must do both. A 5-minute plan should therefore map three sections — the extract, two supporting moments from other staves, and a final sentence linking everything back to Dickens’s argument.

Key Fact

Plan for 5 minutes, write for 40, check for 5. The plan should list: (1) extract thesis, (2) two methods from the extract, (3) two supporting moments from other staves, (4) context strand, (5) closing argument.

Structuring the 40-Mark Answer

Aim for four or five substantial paragraphs plus a sharp conclusion. A strong shape: Introduction (50 words stating Dickens’s argument); Extract paragraph (zoom in on two methods); Supporting paragraph 1 (a scene earlier in the novella); Supporting paragraph 2 (a scene later in the novella); Contextual paragraph; Conclusion (return to the statement given in the question). Treat the introduction as a miniature answer: state your line of argument, name the methods, and signpost context.

Use the authorial voice throughout: “Dickens shows...”, “Dickens suggests...”, “Dickens constructs...”. This automatically signals that you are analysing, not retelling.

Relevant context strands include: the 1834 New Poor Law and workhouses, Thomas Malthus’s ideas about population, Victorian ghost stories as moral warnings, Dickens’s own childhood in a blacking factory, and the Ragged Schools Dickens supported. Irrelevant context includes: biographical trivia about Dickens’s favourite foods, unconnected Victorian inventions, modern ideas of Christmas. The test is always: does this context change how I read the quotation?

Using Short, Embedded Quotations

OCR examiners repeatedly comment that the strongest candidates embed short quotations inside their own sentences rather than drop in long block quotes. Compare: ‘Dickens writes that Scrooge is “hard and sharp as flint”’ reads far weaker than ‘Dickens “flint”-like Scrooge is cold but capable of sparking change.’ Pick a single word or a three- to five-word phrase, slot it into your sentence, then analyse it. Aim for at least eight embedded quotations across a full essay — one or two per paragraph.

Final Checks Before You Submit

Run three final checks on your essay: (1) have you quoted from at least three different staves? (2) have you used the writer’s name at least once per paragraph? (3) does every quotation lead to analysis rather than paraphrase? Answer yes to all three and you are in the top bands. Manage time strictly — finishing a weaker answer beats abandoning a stronger one mid-paragraph. Common pitfalls to avoid: retelling the plot, writing about characters as if they were real, forgetting to use the author’s name, and leaving the conclusion empty or generic.
